title: Reading the Formal -ra: el que fuera presidente

sections.title: What you know, and what is new
sections.content: You know the *-ra* form of the imperfect subjunctive for conditions, wishes and requests. In formal writing, above all in news reports, history and some novels, it sometimes does something else: it works like a past indicative. *El que fuera presidente* means *el que había sido presidente* "the one who had been president". This is a form to **recognise** when you read. You do not need to use it, and in conversation you would say *fue* or *había sido*.

sections.title: The -ra form with the value of a past indicative
rows: the one who had been president (= *el que había sido presidente*)
la ciudad donde naciera el poeta
the city where the poet was born (= *donde nació*)
the book that he published in 1950 (= *que publicó*)
the agreements they had signed then (= *que habían firmado*)

sections.title: How to recognise it
sections.content: How can you tell? Look for three signs. First, the clause states a fact about the past: a person, a place or a thing that really existed, usually named or already known. Second, there is no *si*, no *ojalá*, no *como si* and no verb of wish or request before it. Third, it usually sits in a relative clause (after *que*, *quien* or *donde*) or after *como*. Compare *Si fuera presidente, cambiaría la ley* "If I were president, I would change the law", which is imagined, with *el hombre que fuera presidente en 1948* "the man who had been president in 1948", which is a fact.

items.spanish: Rómulo Gallegos, que fuera presidente de Venezuela en 1948, murió en 1969.
items.english: Rómulo Gallegos, who was president of Venezuela in 1948, died in 1969.

items.spanish: El pueblo donde naciera la escritora es hoy una ciudad grande.
items.english: The town where the writer was born is a large city today.

items.spanish: La cronista recordó el golpe que derrocara al presidente.
items.english: The reporter recalled the coup that had overthrown the president.

sections.content: Only the *-ra* form does this. *Fuese* cannot replace *fuera* in *el que fuera presidente*. You will read this form in the text that closes the unit.
